Colin Reed
Executive Chairman, Ryman Hospitality Properties
Patrick, you wanna do that?
Patrick Chaffin
COO, Ryman Hospitality Properties
Sure. Good morning. We are already substantially through some work at Gaylord Opryland around the Presidential Ballroom and the associated spaces. The ballroom itself is complete, and now we're working through some of the associated spaces around it. That will be completed in June of this year. We have begun work on the space expansion at Gaylord Opryland. That will continue through into 2027. That work has just begun, and that has been comprehended in what Jennifer already shared. We're continuing work on the sports bar, events lawn, and group pavilion in the Magnolia Courtyard at Gaylord Opryland. That will be completed either right at the end of this year or in the first quarter of 2026. We're just watching the weather to determine how that impact will play out.
We'll begin the renovation of our room product at Gaylord Texan in Q2 of this year, and we'll complete that roughly in Q2 of next year.
Ari Klein
Director, Equity Research, BMO Capital Markets
Just on the headwinds that we're seeing in 2025. Is this kind of a peak level you think, or just given some of the longer term plans, you know, maybe that increases.
Patrick Chaffin
COO, Ryman Hospitality Properties
Yeah, I would say that from a disruption perspective, what we've communicated thus far is that we think it's comparable to what we saw in 2024. There's a lot more volume going through in 2025, but we don't expect us to face some of the same headwinds that we saw at the Gaylord Palms room renovation in 2024. More volume, but about the same amount of disruption year over year.
Ari Klein
Director, Equity Research, BMO Capital Markets
Okay. Then just on the higher mix of association business in 2025 impacting out-of-room spend. Curious what that mix looks like in the group bookings in 2026, you know, and 2027, and if maybe we see that trend kind of revert in those years.
Patrick Chaffin
COO, Ryman Hospitality Properties
Yeah, we are moving towards a higher mix of corporate in 2026. Obviously, we still have a lot of business to book into that period of time, but we do see a higher mix of corporate in 2026 based on what's on the books right now. I would point out, though, that even with the higher mix of association in 2025, our rate on the books, from a group perspective is very, very healthy and shows a solid growth. So not all. You know, generally speaking, corporate has better spend outside the room and is a higher premium customer, but we're doing a better and better job of attracting the most premium association groups. I'm very encouraged by what's on the books and how we'll see that play out this year.
Mark Fioravanti
President and CEO, Ryman Hospitality Properties
Hey, Ari, just one thing back on disruption as it relates to the Opryland room, meeting space expansion. This first phase this year is the most disruptive as the demolition occurs. As we roll into 2026, as that project will continue, it will be less disruptive to ongoing business because you'll have less noise interrupting groups.
Patrick Chaffin
COO, Ryman Hospitality Properties
Less connecting of the building. Yep.
Ari Klein
Director, Equity Research, BMO Capital Markets
Appreciate the color. Thank you.
Patrick Chaffin
COO, Ryman Hospitality Properties
Thanks, Ari.
Operator
We'll take our next question from Smedes Rose with Citi. Please go ahead. Your line is open.
Smedes Rose
Director, Citi
Hi. Thank you. I wanted to ask you, a little bit about your labor and wage costs. Maybe how much did they increase in 2024, and how much are you baking in for 2025?
Patrick Chaffin
COO, Ryman Hospitality Properties
Hey, Smedes, this is Patrick. Good morning to you. Yeah, we saw wages specifically year-over-year, we saw about a 3.3% increase, and we're baking in about the same amount, but we did incorporate the full year impact of our collective bargaining agreement with Gaylord National and the union there. We've taken that into account. You know, 3% to 4% expense increase is what we're expecting on the wage and labor front.
Mark Fioravanti
President and CEO, Ryman Hospitality Properties
Basically the same in our entertainment business too. We took big increases back in 2023, 2022, and 2023.
Patrick Chaffin
COO, Ryman Hospitality Properties
We did. I mean, to Colin's point, we're up at the end of 2024. We're up about 34% in the hotel business in terms of wages. The most important thing is our wage margin has remained flat.
Mark Fioravanti
President and CEO, Ryman Hospitality Properties
Yeah.
Patrick Chaffin
COO, Ryman Hospitality Properties
We're very proud of our ability to manage the productivity levels, to offset the increase in wages.
Smedes Rose
Director, Citi
Thanks. I just wanted to ask you know, you've talked about record bookings on, you know, all future room nights, et cetera. Just any sort of change in the profile of who's booking? Is it, you know, are you seeing pickups in associations or trade shows, or is it sort of typical mix or any kind of color you can provide there?
Patrick Chaffin
COO, Ryman Hospitality Properties
Yeah, I would tell you that, you know, part of this investment thesis that we've embarked on is our ability to remix hotels like Gaylord Opryland towards a higher mix of the premium corporate business. I'm really proud of what the Opryland team has been doing, in terms of what they booked in the Q4 and throughout 2024. Opryland achieved the highest growth in ADR of any of our hotels. They are doing a great job of remixing that hotel towards a higher level of corporate. We will always need association business, and we highly value it. In fact, in the DC market, we're trying to get a little bit more association in place because that market just has seen some challenges for the past few years, and our way of offsetting that is securing more association business long term.
Across the brand, we have been seeing a higher mix towards corporate, and a lot of that is a result of the investments we've been making that makes it more palatable for those groups to come to us.
Mark Fioravanti
President and CEO, Ryman Hospitality Properties
Regardless of the segment, we're moving to higher rated groups.
Patrick Chaffin
COO, Ryman Hospitality Properties
Absolutely.
Mark Fioravanti
President and CEO, Ryman Hospitality Properties
Yeah.
Patrick Chaffin
COO, Ryman Hospitality Properties
Yeah. We've intentionally walked away from a few groups in order to achieve those higher rates and said, "This is the investment thesis, and this is the product we have. If you can't afford it, we understand that." You know, some groups have said, "Okay, we're going elsewhere." Then they've come back and said, "No, we'll pay the higher rate to continue to enjoy this experience.
Mark Fioravanti
President and CEO, Ryman Hospitality Properties
Groups that have been with us for 20 years.
Patrick Chaffin
COO, Ryman Hospitality Properties
That's right.
Mark Fioravanti
President and CEO, Ryman Hospitality Properties
Yeah.
Smedes Rose
Director, Citi
All right. Thank you. Appreciate it.
Patrick Chaffin
COO, Ryman Hospitality Properties
Thanks, Smedes Rose.
Operator
We'll take our next question from Duane Pfennigwerth with Evercore ISI. Please go ahead. Your line is open.
Duane Pfennigwerth
Senior Managing Director, Equity Research, Evercore ISI
Hey, hey, thank you. Good morning. Just wondering with respect to, you know, the ICE! results at Gaylord Texan and Gaylord Opryland, is that typically a local market demand, or is that drive-to leisure? You know, do you think there was a trend change in those local markets, or is this more about, you know, ICE! programming, and do you think that could evolve next year?
Mark Fioravanti
President and CEO, Ryman Hospitality Properties
Well, it is more local and, you know, very short drive-in demand. What's unique about the Christmas leisure guest is that it is a much shorter length of stay than our summer guest, but they spend two times the amount on property. It's a, you know, it is a short duration, higher cost activity for the leisure guest. You know, what we saw this year was, you know, those admissions were flat in terms of guests attending ICE!, but what we saw was a decrease in the overnight stay. Some of it looks like it was potentially the lower rated customer trading down from an overnight stay to just a day visit.
We're doing some work around that now to try to understand, you know, exactly what the behavior was, as it relates to those customers.
Patrick Chaffin
COO, Ryman Hospitality Properties
Yeah.
Colin Reed
Executive Chairman, Ryman Hospitality Properties
If I might, Duane, this is Colin. Good morning. I wanna just add something here because, you know, I've read a few reports here this morning that sort of highlights our results as sort of leisure weakness. I wanna put this in perspective. You know, in 2019, these five of our big hotels in 2019 did just under $150 million in revenue in the month of December. In last year, not 2024, 2023, we did about $200 million. It was up 34% from 2019 to 2023, basically all leisure business. In 2024, we did about $192 million, slightly below last year. But these are spectacular numbers. So ICE! is one component of it.
Over the years, we've, you know, built light shows, we do dinner shows, we have kids areas, we have massive indoor pool complexes that drives this leisure business. This is very, very strong business. The weakest of these five hotels did about $1 million a day in revenue in the month of December. Opryland, 2,800 rooms, did $1.75 million a day in basically in leisure business in the month of December. Our leisure business is not weak. Our leisure business is very strong in the month of December. It's just that it wasn't quite as strong as we thought it was gonna be. That all happened in the last couple of weeks. We'll get to the bottom of that. Is it pricing?
You know, is it the consumer is just a little fatigued? My guess it's maybe a little bit of both, and we will figure that out. Our leisure business is very strong.
Patrick Chaffin
COO, Ryman Hospitality Properties
Yeah. I will tell you, just to add to that, we did some primary research with the ICE! consumers as they were exiting ICE!. We did see a lot more economic sensitivity. Now, as a result of that, we softened up and played around a bit with our yielding strategies. We did not see a dramatic improvement in volume sold as a result of lowering price. So we went back to, you know, where we stood from a pricing perspective. Our takeaway from that is there's just a lot of uncertainty and a lot of sensitivity, and so folks were just making decisions to spend less in some of those lower tiered value consumers.
It wasn't that we had priced out of their capability or what they were interested in buying into. It's just that they were very unsure about this season and were being a little more cautious.
Duane Pfennigwerth
Senior Managing Director, Equity Research, Evercore ISI
Thank you. That's helpful context. Just with respect to the group bookings and your momentum with corporates, any particular industries, that stick out? Thanks for taking the questions.
Patrick Chaffin
COO, Ryman Hospitality Properties
Yeah. I would say that we are very interested in financial, and tech and are doubling our efforts to go after some of that. We've seen growth across a lot of industries. Beyond those two, I wouldn't say there's anything that really stands out.
Duane Pfennigwerth
Senior Managing Director, Equity Research, Evercore ISI
Thank you.
Patrick Chaffin
COO, Ryman Hospitality Properties
Thank you.
Operator
We'll take our next question from Dori Kesten with Wells Fargo. Please go ahead. Your line is open.
Dori Kesten
Director, Wells Fargo
Thanks. Good morning. After the Opryland meeting space expansion announcement, are there more announcements like this in the background that you're considering? Or is the CapEx plan that you laid out at the Investor Day through 2027 pretty baked in at this point?
Colin Reed
Executive Chairman, Ryman Hospitality Properties
May-maybe.
Mark Fioravanti
President and CEO, Ryman Hospitality Properties
Well-
Colin Reed
Executive Chairman, Ryman Hospitality Properties
I mean, the way we think about this stuff, Dori, is, you know, we don't wake up and sort of say, "You know what? We need to expand this hotel." We look at the demand characteristics of each of our physical assets. We look at things like turndowns. We look at, you know, all of the activity amongst the meeting planning community. You know, here's the good news, as we've talked about this morning, is that we are building a lot of forward demand into this business. If that forward demand continues to accelerate, there will probably be additional rooms expansions that we will have to and meeting space we'll have to contemplate.
You know, I think we've said many times before, Mark, when we bought Hill Country, you know, we didn't buy Hill Country to have it as approximately a 1,000-room hotel 10 years from now. We believe in inducing demand into that market, and at some point in time, we will pull the trigger. We're in a very interesting and exciting time for this company. I frankly tell you, this is a very exciting time for this company because we are building really strong forward demand because of the unique capabilities of our hotels. I think this will give us the opportunity to deploy more capital at high rates of return over the years to come.
Mark Fioravanti
President and CEO, Ryman Hospitality Properties
Yeah. I think it's fair to say that, you know, all enhancements are not created equal in terms of construction disruption. You know, adding rooms is less disruptive than, say, renovating all of your meeting space. Because when you take meeting space out of inventory, you obviously can't sell into groups. You know, Colin's right. We look at every hotel in terms of, you know, how do we drive incremental profitability, be that through additional rooms, through renovations, or through new food and beverage options, et cetera. And then we'll consider the disruption as part of the returns analysis based on the type of project.
Patrick Chaffin
COO, Ryman Hospitality Properties
You know, Dori, one of the beauties of this new space expansion at Gaylord Opryland is once that's open and you have brand new space, it allows you to take what would've been seen as disruption in the past and absorb it into that new space to get Tennessee Ballroom renovated and the Delta Ballroom re-renovated. There's definitely an agenda with getting this built as quickly as possible so that we can not create additional disruption when we need to do other renovations at that hotel.
Dori Kesten
Director, Wells Fargo
Yeah.
Jennifer Hutcheson
CFO, Ryman Hospitality Properties
Dori, I think the only other project that was on the page that we've talked about in recent years, in addition to, you know, what everyone else has mentioned is the Rockies expansion. I think that's always been in the background as something we view as, you know, part of the long-term view, but there's still a few things to work through on the design and-
Colin Reed
Executive Chairman, Ryman Hospitality Properties
Yeah
Jennifer Hutcheson
CFO, Ryman Hospitality Properties
other issues.
Colin Reed
Executive Chairman, Ryman Hospitality Properties
I would say we're probably nearer today to that one than we were 12, 18 months ago, simply because of what we've been able to accomplish with the complete beautification of that Grand Lodge and the food and beverage and the impact that we're seeing on those investments that we've made have got us, you know, pretty excited about Colorado.
Patrick Chaffin
COO, Ryman Hospitality Properties
Yeah, we've just got some administrative.
Colin Reed
Executive Chairman, Ryman Hospitality Properties
Yeah.
Patrick Chaffin
COO, Ryman Hospitality Properties
Political issues to work through there.
Mark Fioravanti
President and CEO, Ryman Hospitality Properties
Yeah.
Dori Kesten
Director, Wells Fargo
It's fair. Thank you for all that. It's fair to say, though, that with the Rockies expansion, that's relative, it's relatively not disruptive, though, just given that it's off to-
Patrick Chaffin
COO, Ryman Hospitality Properties
Yeah.
Dori Kesten
Director, Wells Fargo
the side.
Patrick Chaffin
COO, Ryman Hospitality Properties
Dori, that's very fair because you're talking about a building that has only one connection point to the main building, and essentially that work can be done almost in complete isolation from the rest of the hotel.
Dori Kesten
Director, Wells Fargo
Okay. Got it. Thank you.
Colin Reed
Executive Chairman, Ryman Hospitality Properties
Thank you.
Operator
We'll take our next question from Chris Darling with Green Street. Please go ahead. Your line is open.
Chris Darling
Senior Analyst, Head of US Lodging, and Gaming Research, Green Street
Thank you. Good morning. A couple questions for you on the Gaylord National. First, what's your expectation for performance in 2025? Secondly, how reliant is that property on the local DC market in terms of demand generation? Just wondering if there's any risk maybe with some of the government efficiency initiatives, and how that may or may not impact that property going forward.
Jennifer Hutcheson
CFO, Ryman Hospitality Properties
I know Patrick's gonna pull up some additional details on that, but we don't generally provide guidance by property level. We can give you some directional color.
Colin Reed
Executive Chairman, Ryman Hospitality Properties
The forward bookings on National for this year, next year, and the year after look pretty good.
Patrick Chaffin
COO, Ryman Hospitality Properties
Yeah. You know, as I mentioned earlier, we do see and are concerned with what's going on from a government perspective, and we've been trying to pivot away from that business as much as possible. I would say we have minimal exposure as we move through 2025. We've already looked at what's on the books and take a look at that. We are trying to mix it towards a higher level of association, because we do think that there's some short-term demand generation challenges in that market. I wouldn't say there's an over-reliance on the local market. There's certainly not from a transient perspective. That hotel runs a much higher percentage of group business than our other hotels, simply because we've found that there's greater strength in being able to drive from the group side.
You know, we believe that, you know, National just finished an incredibly strong year in terms of performance and will continue that trend.
Chris Darling
Senior Analyst, Head of US Lodging, and Gaming Research, Green Street
But-
Operator
Okay. Go ahead.
Mark Fioravanti
President and CEO, Ryman Hospitality Properties
Chris, it's fair to say that, you know, all the headlines we're seeing now around, you know, some of the political changes that are occurring. We're considering that across the portfolio as we think about, you know, group exposure and what business, you know, we either have on the books or we're pursuing and how it might affect their behavior.
Chris Darling
Senior Analyst, Head of US Lodging, and Gaming Research, Green Street
Okay. That's all helpful thoughts. I have a bit of a nuanced question. There may not be a lot here, but I'll ask it anyway. You know, you mentioned you come into this year expecting lower out-of-room spend or a little bit lower out-of-room spend because of the group mix shift. I wonder, you know, with that dynamic in place, what's your ability to sort of manage your expense structure around that? Is there anything to read into about that?
Patrick Chaffin
COO, Ryman Hospitality Properties
Well, I mean, obviously, that is a high margin piece of our business, but that's been taken into account in the guidance that we've provided, and there are other levers that we pull to try and offset maybe a mix shift from corporate to association. To my point earlier, you know, we do see the room rate on the books is in very strong position, and our sales teams do an excellent job of, you know, when they're 90 days out or 30 days out from a group arriving, of trying to upsell every single group to try and drive additional spend outside the room. You know, generally, we have a number of levers that we put into place to try and offset that and to maintain our margin or even grow it.
Jennifer Hutcheson
CFO, Ryman Hospitality Properties
Just to put this in context too, I mean, the association mix that we're seeing on the books is comparable to what we've seen in prior periods. We just had a really strong mix of corporate in 2024 as well. Just again, to put the context, put all that into context.
Mark Fioravanti
President and CEO, Ryman Hospitality Properties
Yeah. It's not a dramatic shift. The thing I was going to add is that one of the advantages of the group business is that with the forward visibility of their activities, you know, from a labor scheduling standpoint, it gives you some advantages because you know where that group's going to be. Are they gonna be in the outlets? Are they gonna be in the banquet meeting rooms? It allows you to more appropriately staff for the volumes.
Patrick Chaffin
COO, Ryman Hospitality Properties
I mean, we just traveled a very large association through Gaylord Opryland this past weekend, and the initial preliminary figures coming back is that the group achieved a historic level of attendance, significantly even outpacing what they did last year, which was historic. As a result, we saw rises in parking, food and beverage outlets, catering across the board. Again, association business generally is not to the same level of premium as corporate. If we see the kind of performance that we saw this weekend, from one of the groups that traveled through Opryland, that bodes well for us.
Colin Reed
Executive Chairman, Ryman Hospitality Properties
Let me take a minute here if I could, and I'm gonna do something here, Patrick, that's gonna surprise you. I'm gonna compliment you and your team. The other thing that I feel very good about our team here, we don't play a passive role with our manager. We play a very active role with our manager. Patrick and his team, you know, literally in these hotels, I mean, basically daily, managing with the managers the cost structure of these businesses. That's one of the reasons why I think over the last two, three years that we've had, you know, very good results around margin, even with wage pressures that we experienced in 2022 and 2023. I will compliment our asset management team.
When we see these mix shifts, we're bringing this to the attention to the leadership of each of these hotels to make sure that we're adjusting our cost structures so that we do not see dilution in our EBITDA margins.
Mark Fioravanti
President and CEO, Ryman Hospitality Properties
Yeah. I mean, to your point, Colin, we had 2.1% same store revenue growth last year, and we grew margins 30 basis points.
Colin Reed
Executive Chairman, Ryman Hospitality Properties
Yeah. Yeah. You know, I don't think it's because of the brilliance of our manager. I think it's a combination of the work that Patrick and his team do daily in the managing of the cost structures of these businesses. That was a compliment, Patrick.
Patrick Chaffin
COO, Ryman Hospitality Properties
Yeah. Thank you. Thank you. Now to Collin's point, there are levers that we pull to maintain the margin on the bottom line, and we've already taken significant steps to get ahead of any risk that we foresee for this year, and impact the bottom line in a positive way to help ourselves out in achieving our goals.
Colin Reed
Executive Chairman, Ryman Hospitality Properties
Does that help, Chris?
Chris Darling
Senior Analyst, Head of US Lodging, and Gaming Research, Green Street
All right. Yeah, it's been a very helpful comment, so I appreciate all the color there. Thank you.
Colin Reed
Executive Chairman, Ryman Hospitality Properties
Thank you.
Operator
We'll take our ne-
Colin Reed
Executive Chairman, Ryman Hospitality Properties
Who? Who's next, David?
Operator
Yep. We'll take our next question from Jay Kornreich with Wedbush Securities. Please go ahead. Your line is open.
Jay Kornreich
VP, REIT Equity Research, Wedbush Securities
Hi. Thanks so much. I wanted to ask about just the pace of group revenue on the books for 2026 being up 11%, which I believe you said reflects ADR growth of 4.5%. I'm curious, as we get closer to 2026 and you're able to book into many of the finished CapEx projects and you've outlined a rate-driven strategy, do you think there's an opportunity to push that 4.5% rate growth even higher?
Mark Fioravanti
President and CEO, Ryman Hospitality Properties
Yes, certainly there is. You know, keep in mind when you look at where revenue on the books is relative to, you know, prior years as we approach the travel date, right? We're moving towards a 50-50 points of occupancy on the books. As we enter a year, typically the differential in revenue on the books is going to be purely rate, typically. That's the opportunity. The opportunity is to continue to push that rate and grow that 6% higher as we move towards the year. Because as the booking window shortens, you're also gonna book more and more corporate business, which typically travels at a higher rate.
Patrick Chaffin
COO, Ryman Hospitality Properties
Just to add to that, I would tell you that the hotels are going through right now because they are ahead and more aggressively, what we call cutting the group room blocks, which is lowering the expectations of how much we'll travel, so that they free up more space and more rooms to sell into. With that compression, they can sell it at higher rates. They are all over it. Revenue management is working to use that compression to drive more room nights and higher rates.
Jay Kornreich
VP, REIT Equity Research, Wedbush Securities
All right. Appreciate that. That's helpful. Just one more on the entertainment segment. You made a number of significant strides over the past year, opening up the Old Red Las Vegas, repositioning to Category 10, you know, a major renovation at Block 21. Just curious if you have any other material investment or expansion plans over the next year or two that you could highlight on the entertainment side.
Colin Reed
Executive Chairman, Ryman Hospitality Properties
You know, the thing that we're most excited about is our investment in Southern Entertainment as another live venue opportunity. That's a really sort of an effective platform for light sort of capital intensity and provides access to really interesting entertainment market destinations, pardon me, and a fan base that complements our existing fan base across the Ryman, The Opry, and Austin City Limits in Austin, Texas.
Mark Fioravanti
President and CEO, Ryman Hospitality Properties
I would say, Jay, it is fair to say that there are a number of things that we're working on that, you know, basically at this point in time, we're not prepared to talk about. There are a lot of different opportunities that we're looking at as it relates to that business.
Colin Reed
Executive Chairman, Ryman Hospitality Properties
I think the challenge is really more prioritization, you know, of what opportunity we focus on.
Jay Kornreich
VP, REIT Equity Research, Wedbush Securities
Okay. Understood. Thank you.
Colin Reed
Executive Chairman, Ryman Hospitality Properties
Thank you.
Operator
We'll take our next question from Chris Woronka with Deutsche Bank. Please go ahead. Your line is open.
Chris Woronka [Senior Analyst
Hotel / Lodging REITs, and Leisure] (Deutsche Bank)
Hey, good morning, everyone. Thanks for squeezing me in on the questions. So I guess maybe we're beating a horse that we didn't expect to be beating. If I can kind of go back to the corporate, you're making all these investments, you know, and partly to attract a hot, more premium corporate group customer, right? I guess, is there any way to frame up how that ideal premium corporate customer looks like versus association or even a kind of a non-premium corporate group, whether it's, you know, size or length of stay or rate or out-of-room spend? You know, if it's smaller, does that...
You know, do we have to think about it being harder potentially to fill some of these leisure weekend spots, or are there more, you know, shoulder periods? Any color you can add would be great. Thank you.
Patrick Chaffin
COO, Ryman Hospitality Properties
Hey, Chris, this is Patrick. So let's hit a couple of things that you mentioned. Corporate rate is generally higher. It's hard to put a specific percentage or number on that. Just generally, on average, it is higher. Outside the room spend, though, is significantly higher with many of those corporate groups. We've seen, you know, levels of $500 or $600 per person spend outside the room per day with some of these corporate customers. That is a tremendously strong number. To the size question, they're not materially different. You would think that, well, your associations are gonna be massive. There's lots of different corporate customers, lots of different group sizes, but there are a lot of corporate groups out there that are very large, are growing, and constantly encouraging us to grow with them.
I can think of three of our top customers who are constantly asking me, "When are you gonna expand Opryland? When are you gonna expand National? When are you" They're constantly looking for us to expand further because they have more of their book of business they would like to turn over to us. They are extremely valuable to us. It is generally a higher rate. It is usually a very solid outside the room spend. From a sizing perspective, there's really no difference because it's such a large universe of groups that you can choose from.
Colin Reed
Executive Chairman, Ryman Hospitality Properties
Our purchase of Hill Country as well has helped us sort of think about the opportunity here with this higher rated corporate business. Because when you look at the rate differential between what is being accomplished in that hotel versus our existing hotels, there's quite a bit of difference. That is exciting stuff for us.
Mark Fioravanti
President and CEO, Ryman Hospitality Properties
I think it's important, Chris, just to recognize that what we're talking about is we're talking about incremental change at the margin. We're not talking wholesale change. You know, we'll continue to have a substantial book of association business. I also think it's important to repeat that, you know, our goal here is to move the rate across all of our segments and to attract and drive and sell to higher rated business, whether that's corporate business, association business or SMERF business.
Patrick Chaffin
COO, Ryman Hospitality Properties
What this really comes down to is us increasing our skill and capability at stacking groups in with one another so that they still feel that they have a unique experience, but that we fill the house in a more optimal way.
Colin Reed
Executive Chairman, Ryman Hospitality Properties
You know, at the end of the day, we have such a small share of this market, you know? We're retaining so many of our customers, and that's what's driving these expansions to move our share up marginally. This is a very interesting time for us.
Patrick Chaffin
COO, Ryman Hospitality Properties
Yeah.
Colin Reed
Executive Chairman, Ryman Hospitality Properties
Chris, any other questions?
Chris Woronka [Senior Analyst
Hotel / Lodging REITs, and Leisure] (Deutsche Bank)
No. I really appreciate all that color. Very helpful. Thanks. Thanks, guys.
Colin Reed
Executive Chairman, Ryman Hospitality Properties
Thanks, buddy.
Operator
We'll take our-
Colin Reed
Executive Chairman, Ryman Hospitality Properties
Yeah.
Operator
We'll take our next question from John DeCree with CBRE. Please go ahead. Your line is open.
John DeCree
Director Equity Research, CBRE
Thank you. Good morning, all. Maybe just one question. I think in prepared remarks, Jennifer, you talked a little bit about some of the conservatism that's built into the low end of the guidance. I'm curious, you know, if you could talk to some of the variables that you'd think about that might get you to the high end of the guidance. I imagine some of that is just leisure and economic variation to expectations, but, you know, maybe there's some ability to manage disruption. Yeah, that's my question. That's all. Thank you.
Jennifer Hutcheson
CFO, Ryman Hospitality Properties
No, I think you hit it on all the areas that we identified that could drive the potential upside, and a lot of that is the variability in leisure. We have less, you know, visibility earlier on into that. On the group side, we know what's on the books and it, you know, to the extent that we can see better performance from the leisure guest, that can help get us to, you know, at the top end, what we have outlined in the guidance.
John DeCree
Director Equity Research, CBRE
Yeah, I would.
Mark Fioravanti
President and CEO, Ryman Hospitality Properties
On the construction disruption side, I would just say that, you know, we've made a lot of enhancements to our design and construction team over this past, you know, eight months or so, as well as processes in terms of some of the vendors and supply chains we use, et cetera. I think that, you know, we feel confident in our ability to manage the disruption going forward. To your point, I think to the extent that we can, you know, improve on kind of what we've outlined, you know, that is, that's potential upside as well.
John DeCree
Director Equity Research, CBRE
Great. Thank you very much. I appreciate it.
Colin Reed
Executive Chairman, Ryman Hospitality Properties
Okay. David, I think one more question. We're almost at the top of the hour.
Operator
Perfect. We'll take our last question from David Katz with Jefferies. Please go ahead. Your line is open.
David Katz
Managing Director, Jefferies LLC
Thanks very much. Made it in under the wire. I wanted to just get your perspective on, you know, Mark, you said it earlier, you know, we're talking about some change on the margin, whether, you know, there. You know, I think everybody's sort of trying to circle some of the drivers of what we're, you know, what we're processing. You know, is there any competition in certain markets, right? You know, any, you know, anything you could point to? I ask the question in context. I know your properties, and there really is nothing quite like them. You know, is there any marginal competition we might be able to point to that may be having some impact?
Mark Fioravanti
President and CEO, Ryman Hospitality Properties
I'm sitting here running through the markets in my head. You know, there's nothing being built.
Patrick Chaffin
COO, Ryman Hospitality Properties
There's nothing being built. Obviously, the JWs that we see in certain markets are competitive. I mean, it's individual assets, some of the Marriott Marquis.
Mark Fioravanti
President and CEO, Ryman Hospitality Properties
Mondo.
Patrick Chaffin
COO, Ryman Hospitality Properties
Yeah.
Colin Reed
Executive Chairman, Ryman Hospitality Properties
Those hotels are not transforming themselves. They are.
Patrick Chaffin
COO, Ryman Hospitality Properties
That's correct. There's a very.
Colin Reed
Executive Chairman, Ryman Hospitality Properties
They're running themselves the way they've historically run themselves. No, I wouldn't.
Mark Fioravanti
President and CEO, Ryman Hospitality Properties
I don't think there's anything new coming on.
Colin Reed
Executive Chairman, Ryman Hospitality Properties
No.
Mark Fioravanti
President and CEO, Ryman Hospitality Properties
I mean, the only product that looks like ours that's coming on is Gaylord Pacific.
Colin Reed
Executive Chairman, Ryman Hospitality Properties
Yeah.
Mark Fioravanti
President and CEO, Ryman Hospitality Properties
Right? That's part of the rotation.
Patrick Chaffin
COO, Ryman Hospitality Properties
It's more motivated by our own internal drive to try and figure out how to enhance and drive growth for the future for our portfolio, not because we're feeling pressure from someone else. We see the opportunity with where groups are growing, where the opportunity lies to remix and on the margin and enhance our revenue picture, and we're pursuing that, not because someone's putting pressure on us.
Mark Fioravanti
President and CEO, Ryman Hospitality Properties
Yeah, David, my comment as it relates to the change at the margin is that what I was trying to communicate was that the goal here is not to go to 80% or 90% corporate, right? We're trying to move it, you know, four or five points. You know.
Patrick Chaffin
COO, Ryman Hospitality Properties
Literally.
Mark Fioravanti
President and CEO, Ryman Hospitality Properties
You know, that type of mix change. That type of mix change can improve profit dramatically.
David Katz
Managing Director, Jefferies LLC
Understood. Appreciate it. Thanks so much.
Colin Reed
Executive Chairman, Ryman Hospitality Properties
Thank you, David.
Mark Fioravanti
President and CEO, Ryman Hospitality Properties
Thanks, David.
Colin Reed
Executive Chairman, Ryman Hospitality Properties
Thank you. Well, David, thank you for presiding over this morning, and we appreciate our investors, analysts being on this call. If there are any questions that you have, follow-up questions, you know how to get a hold of our IR team, Jennifer Hutcheson or Mark. Thank you, and we'll see you soon.
Operator
This does conclude today's program. Thank you for your participation, and you may now disconnect.
